history.heading: Kingdom of Burundi
paragraphs: Burundi, a small landlocked country in the hills of the African Great Lakes region, was home to Twa, Hutu and Tutsi peoples. From the 17th century a kingdom developed under a mwami (king), with a complex social hierarchy in which princely lineages known as ganwa held power.
The kingdom remained independent until the end of the 19th century and resisted early German incursions.

history.heading: Colonial rule
paragraphs: Burundi became part of German East Africa in the 1890s. After the First World War it was administered by Belgium together with Rwanda as Ruanda-Urundi. Belgian rule relied on the Tutsi elite and hardened distinctions between Hutu and Tutsi, including through identity cards.

history.heading: Independence and conflict
paragraphs: Burundi became independent on 1 July 1962 as a monarchy, which was overthrown in 1966. A series of Tutsi-dominated military regimes followed. Massacres of Hutu in 1972 killed between 100,000 and 300,000 people.

In 1993 Melchior Ndadaye, the first Hutu president, was assassinated months after his election, triggering a civil war that killed around 300,000 people. The Arusha Agreement of 2000 and subsequent ceasefires introduced power-sharing between Hutu and Tutsi. Pierre Nkurunziza's decision to seek a third term in 2015 led to a political crisis, a failed coup and repression.

culture.heading: Drums and traditions
paragraphs: Kirundi is the national language, spoken by nearly everyone, which is unusual in Africa; French and English are also official. Most people are Christian, mainly Catholic.

The Royal Drum ritual dance, with dancers beating large drums carried on their heads, is recognised by UNESCO and is a powerful national symbol. Common foods include beans, bananas, cassava and sweet potatoes.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Burundi is a presidential republic. The constitution includes ethnic quotas in government and parliament as part of the post-war settlement. The CNDD-FDD party, which emerged from a Hutu rebel group, has dominated politics since 2005.
Human rights groups report restrictions on opposition, media and civil society. Burundi has sent troops to eastern DR Congo, and tensions with Rwanda have been high.

economy.heading: One of the poorest countries
paragraphs: Burundi is one of the poorest countries in the world, with most people relying on subsistence farming on small plots in a very densely populated country. Coffee and tea are the main exports.

The economy has suffered from conflict, isolation and shortages of fuel and foreign currency. The currency is the Burundian franc. Burundi has deposits of nickel and rare earths that are largely undeveloped.
